Gallows
GAL-ohz
noun
From the Anglo-Saxon galga, a cross or gibbet; in Esther it renders the Hebrew 'ets, “tree” or “timber,” the Persian stake of fifty cubits on which Haman purposed to hang Mordecai and on which he was himself hanged.

Biblical Definition

The gallows of Scripture belongs to the book of Esther, and it is the hinge on which the whole providence of that book turns. Haman, full of wrath because one Jew would not bow, was counselled by his wife and friends: “Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon” (Est 5:14). The thing pleased him, and he built it — seventy-five feet of deliberate spite, raised in his own courtyard so that the whole city might see his enemy die. That same night the king could not sleep, and the book of the records was read, and Haman was made to lead through the street the man he had come to destroy. Then Harbonah, who had noticed the timber standing in Haman’s house, named it before the king (Est 7:9), and the sentence came in five words: Hang him thereon. “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Est 7:10). Afterward his ten sons were hanged upon it also (Est 9:25). The name of God is never spoken in Esther, and He is never absent from a line of it. The gallows is the standing monument of Psa 7:15 — “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” — and of the law that the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands.

Webster 1828 Definition

An instrument of execution consisting of an upright timber, or two with a cross-beam, on which criminals are hanged; in Esther, Haman’s stake of fifty cubits.

expand to see more

GALLOWS, an instrument of punishment, on which criminals are put to death by hanging.

It consists usually of two posts and a cross-beam on the top.

From the Saxon galga, a cross or gibbet; the same root appears in the Gothic galga.

In Scripture, the Hebrew is 'ets, a tree or timber, hence a stake set upright (Est 5:14).

Proverbially, the fate a man prepares for another and himself receives.

Key Scripture

Est 5:14 — "Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made."

Est 7:9 — "And Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon."

Est 7:10 — "So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king’s wrath pacified."

Est 9:25 — "But when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows."

Modern Corruption

The reversal is flattened into “karma,” “poetic justice,” or mere irony — an impersonal cosmic balance replacing the God who governs sleepless nights, court records, and the tongue of a chamberlain.

expand to see more

Haman’s end is one of the best-known reversals in literature, and it is almost always told as irony: the schemer hoist with his own petard, the universe evening the score. That reading is a theft of agency. Karma is an impersonal law working through fate; providence is a Person working through second causes. Esther names none of the causes as miracles — a king’s insomnia, a reader picking one page of the chronicles, a queen’s invitation to a second banquet, a chamberlain who happened to have seen a timber in a courtyard — and every one of them lands exactly where it must for a nation to be spared and one man to be hanged. The book withholds the name of God precisely so that the reader will learn to see His hand where His name is not written, which is the ordinary condition of every day we live. To call it irony is to admire the pattern while denying the weaver.

Recover both halves of the doctrine. First, the moral government of God is real and inescapable: “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psa 7:15); the mischief returns upon a man’s own head and his violent dealing comes down upon his own pate. Vengeance is the LORD’s, and He does not need our help to execute it — Mordecai never lifted a hand against Haman, and neither should the Christian who is being schemed against. Second, and greater, there is one gallows in Scripture on which the innocent hung in the guilty’s room. Haman got what he deserved on his own timber; Christ took what we deserved on His, made a curse for us, as it is written, cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. Every deserved execution in Scripture points by contrast to the one undeserved death that saves, and there the wrath of the King was pacified for ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ets, “tree, timber,” the upright stake of Persian execution; the English word is Saxon galga, a gibbet or cross, and the Greek renders the Hebrew with the ordinary word for wood.

expand to see more

Hebrew — 'ets (עץ), tree, wood, timber; in Esther an upright stake for impaling or hanging.

Hebrew — talah (תלה), to hang up, the verb used of Haman and of the bodies exposed under Deu 21:22-23.

Greek — xulon (ξύλον), wood or tree, the New Testament word for the cross in Act 5:30 and Gal 3:13.

Saxon — galga, a gibbet or cross; the English gallows is a plural form long used as a singular.

Measure — fifty cubits is roughly seventy-five feet; the height was pride, not necessity.

Usage

"“He built the gallows in his own courtyard, and it was the last thing he ever built.”"

"“The book never names God, and there is not a page of it He is absent from.”"

"“Haman hung on the timber he deserved; Christ hung on one He did not.”"
